questions.question: How do you implement a stack and queue using Go slices?
questions.title: Slice As Stack And Queue
questions.direct_answer: Stack: append (push) and slice-to-last (pop) — LIFO. Queue: append (push) and slice-from-first (pop) — FIFO, but the naive front-pop copies (or leaks memory) — the proper Go queue uses a head index or a ring buffer.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Stack: append (push) and slice-to-last (pop) — LIFO. Queue: append (push) and slice-from-first (pop) — FIFO, but the naive front-pop copies (or leaks memory) — the proper Go queue uses a head index or a ring buffer.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The stack, executed:
```go
stack := []int{}
stack = append(stack, 1)     // push
stack = append(stack, 2)
top := stack[len(stack)-1]     // peek: 2
stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]    // pop: 2, stack=[1]
```

The queue — naive (the trap):
```go
queue := []int{}
queue = append(queue, 1)
queue = append(queue, 2)
front := queue[0]              // peek: 1
queue = queue[1:]               // pop — PROBLEM
```

The naive pop's problem: queue[1:] copies the remaining elements (or the old array stays alive until GC — either O(n) per pop or a memory leak pattern). For 1M elements, each pop moves 1M-1.

The proper queue — head index:
```go
type Queue struct {
    items []int
    head  int
}
func (q *Queue) Push(v int) { q.items = append(q.items, v) }
func (q *Queue) Pop() int {
    v := q.items[q.head]
    q.head++
    if q.head > len(q.items)/2 {  // compact occasionally
        q.items = q.items[q.head:]
        q.head = 0
    }
    return v
}
```

The head-index pattern: pop increments head (O(1)), and the compaction (a copy) happens every half — amortized O(1). The idiomatic Go queue.

The list alternative: container/list (doubly-linked) or a channel (bounded, blocking) — the right tool when the slice's copy-on-compaction matters.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Stack: append + s:len-1] --> L[LIFO — last in, first out]
    Q[Queue: append + s:0 or head++] --> F[FIFO — first in, first out]
    Q2[head-index queue] --> AM[amortized O1 per op]
    C[chan T, size] --> B[bounded, blocking, goroutine-safe]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The stack's slice mechanics: append amortizes (the grow-by-double — the slices topic); the pop is a header update (len decreases — no copy). Both ends O(1) amortized — the slice IS a good stack. The memory subtlety: the underlying array keeps capacity — a stack that grows huge then empties holds the array until GC sees the reference go. For a long-running server's reusable stack, pre-allocate and manage the length yourself.

The queue's amortized analysis: the head-index compact pattern does a copy of size n/2 every n/2 pops — each pop's average cost is (n/2 copy)/(n/2 pops) = O(1). The alternative trigger — 'when head equals len' (fully drained) — avoids the copy entirely but requires the Push to reset — the two forms have the same amortized bound.

The channel-as-queue (the Go-specific option): make(chan int, bufferSize) — a bounded, thread-safe queue with blocking semantics. The right answer when the queue is between goroutines (the producer/consumer pattern) — the channel IS the concurrency-safe queue. For single-goroutine use, the slice is faster; the channel adds synchronization you don't need.
